item.title: Saudi defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan is a verdict on American reliability
item.description: It’s an insurance policy taken out by governments that no longer wish to entrust their safety to a single guarantor.
item.content:encoded:
Commentators predictably reacted to the news of the signing of a mutual defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan on August 7 by reaching for the label “Islamic Nato”. The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement stipulates that an armed attack on any one of them would be treated as an attack on all. Jerusalem went a step further, describing the alliance as an anti-Israel alliance.

But the Nato comparison is the wrong framing. Three of America’s own partners have bound themselves together – and the most consequential audience for what they signed sits not in Tehran or Tel Aviv but in Washington. The agreement reads, in effect, as a verdict on American reliability.

On paper, the combination is formidable. Turkey fields Nato’s second-largest army and a drone industry that has reshaped modern battlefields. Saudi Arabia brings the Gulf’s deepest reserves of capital. Pakistan adds a large, combat-experienced military and the Muslim world’s only nuclear arsenal. Analysts point to genuinely complementary assets here: Turkish technology which is short of markets, Pakistani manpower short of financing, Saudi wealth short of manpower.

This pact did not appear from nowhere. It extends a Saudi-Pakistani agreement of September 2025, signed days after Israel’s strike on Hamas targets in Doha, Qatar, and was made more urgent by the US-Israeli war...

It withdrew the decision a few hours later, but said it had sought an inquiry report from the university identifying those who were “principally instrumental” in opposing Kant’s participation in the convocation.

Later in the night, the council closed all proceedings against the students, saying it was satisfied that the 2026 batch had no role in any “disturbance or movement”.

The matter was mentioned on Friday before a bench comprising Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana after Advocate K Parameshwar challenged the council’s action.

item.title: In Bangladesh, jute mandate can’t stop switch to plastic sacks
item.description: Synthetic fibres have made inroads due to easy availability and low cost.
item.content:encoded:
Bangladesh is the world’s second largest producer of the environmentally friendly fiber jute. However, the country has, for decades, grappled with the move to combat the escalating use of the cheaper and more popular, but harmful, plastic-based packaging and synthetic fibers.

As a safeguard measure, the government, 16 years ago, enacted a law for the mandatory use of jute sacks and bags to contain and carry 19 essential commodities, including rice, wheat and fertiliser.

The move has been largely unsuccessful, though, with plastic and synthetic fiber invasion as packaging ingredients continuing unabated. Synthetic and poly bags have caused environmental problems such as waste disposal.

Nazmul Haque, the government-appointed jute officer in the northern Sherpur district, told Mongabay that a small semi-automatic rice mill – Sakhina Rice Mill – has exclusively been using jute sacks.

Sakhina Rice Mill in Sherpur stands out from the crowd by exclusively using jute bags and sacks, debunking the narratives of fellow rice millers that jute sacks and bags reduce their profit margin.

Companies selling packaged food products in India often claim that they are healthy, natural, pure, sugar-free – but are they actually so?

In 2024, a committee of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India reviewed more than 160 food products that had been flagged for making misleading claims. Two years later, our investigation found a majority of those claims were still in circulation.

item.title: Manipur: Two Nagas killed in firing by militants at Kangpokpi
item.description: The Liangmai Naga Council-Manipur announced an immediate total shutdown of Liangmai Naga-inhabited areas of Manipur until further notice.
item.content:encoded:
Two Naga persons were killed in firing by suspected militants in Manipur’s Kangpokpi district on Friday, Ukhrul Times reported.

A group of men armed with “sophisticated weapons” attacked Langka Naga village at around 8 am, an unidentified police officer told PTI.

The officer said that a man identified as W Chawang died at the scene after suffering gunshot wounds to the head, while three others were injured.

The second person who died has been identified as Kawidinang Abonmai, India Today NE reported.

Residents said that an armed group from the Naga village also opened fire at the suspected attackers following the incident, PTI reported.

The Liangmai Naga Council-Manipur condemned the attack and alleged that militants from the Kuki National Front (P) were behind it.

The council announced an immediate total shutdown of Liangmai Naga-inhabited areas of Manipur until further notice.

It said shops, officers institutions and non-essential activities would remain closed, while medical, fire and other emergency services would be exempted.

It also appealed to residents to remain calm and urged the authorities to ensure public safety and bring those responsible to justice.

item.title: Romance fiction: Online drama complicates a young couple’s relationship
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Days with My Red-Flag Girlfriend’, by Kajol Aikat.
item.content:encoded:
Every good love story includes a Holi celebration.

But personally, I never felt the festival was romantic in any conventional sense. It’s loud, anarchic and someone always gets colour in their mouth. The thandai is spiked by someone who doesn’t announce it. The white clothes you wore, ironically, are destroyed within four minutes. Someone’s playlist is terrible. Someone’s playlist is perfect. It doesn’t matter. But maybe that’s the point.

Holi felt better that year.

The festivities happened on the college lawn, which had been transformed overnight into something between a fever dream and a Bollywood set that had run out of budget but not enthusiasm. There was colour everywhere – powder smeared on the walls, footprints of pink and green tracking across the concrete, clouds of dry gulal drifting through the air like slow, festive smoke. Some guy from the third floor had dragged a JBL speaker the size of a small refrigerator down four flights of stairs purely for this moment, and it was playing “Genda Phool” at a volume that suggested he felt the song had never been heard at its true potential before.

Buckets of water arced through the air with no warning. Someone had knocked thandai over the DJ’s laptop....

item.title: Tata Group Chairman N Chandrasekaran has resigned. How did the group start its ‘swadeshi’ business?
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Tata: The Global Corporation That Built Indian Capitalism’, by Mircea Raianu.
item.content:encoded:
Early in 1864, a young Parsi merchant from Bombay named Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata set sail for ­ England, carry­ing a set of bills of exchange backed by a consignment of Indian cotton. By the time the ship docked in Liverpool, the price of cotton had fallen so quickly that the bills became worthless. Un- expectedly forced to manage the liquidation of his ­ father’s firm, Jamsetji took time to observe the workings of the textile mills in Lancashire, the heartland of the Industrial Revolution. When he returned to India a few months ­ later, he found Bombay in the grip of a disastrous financial crisis. The ­ whole of the city, Jamsetji’s first biographer ­ later recalled, “was sitting on the stool of repentance, with sackcloth and ashes; while the disconsolate creditors held Dharma at the door of their ruined debtors.” Out of this chastening experience arose India’s own Industrial Revolution, more modest and ­ limited in scope than its British counterpart but all the more impressive for the constraints it had to overcome.

item.title: SC stays Madras HC order quashing government jobs for kin of Karur stampede victims
item.description: The lawyers appearing for the state submitted that the government was within its powers to grant compassionate appointments as a policy decision.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Friday stayed the Madras High Court ruling striking down a Tamil Nadu government order granting government jobs on compassionate grounds to the family members of the persons who died in the Karur stampede, Live Law reported.

The stampede took place on September 27 at Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam chief Vijay’s rally in Karur district when he was addressing supporters from his campaign vehicle. Forty-one persons had died in the stampede.

Vijay went on to become the chief minister of Tamil Nadu on May 10 after his party became the single-largest party in the Assembly elections.

A bench comprising Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran passed the interim order on Friday while issuing notice on a petition filed by the state and others challenging the High Court’s judgement.

The lawyers appearing for the state submitted that the government was within its powers to grant compassionate appointments as a policy decision, the legal news outlet reported.

“A stampede took place. An unfortunate incident happened,” Bar and Bench quoted the court as saying. “The government has decided to compensate them. Should the government not give employment?” it added.

item.title: Delhi HC, airport, several other sites receive bomb threats ahead of Independence Day
item.description: Nothing suspicious had been found so far, officials said.
item.content:encoded:
Multiple locations in Delhi, including the High Court and Terminal 3 of Indira Gandhi International Airport, received bomb threats on Friday, a day ahead of Independence Day, The Hindu reported.

The Delhi High Court received a threatening email with the subject line “Bomb Blast Delhi High Court @ 2:11PM”. The email warned of a blast at the High Court premises at 2.11 pm on Saturday, followed by explosions at district courts in the national capital at 3.11pm, the newspaper reported.

Threats were also received at Jamnagar House, the Jhandewalan Flatted Factory Complex, the district magistrate’s office in Saket and the sub-divisional magistrate’s office in Delhi Cantonment, ANI quoted the Delhi Fire Services as saying.

Police, bomb disposal teams, fire department personnel, dog squads and other security agencies carried out searches at the sites, The Indian Express reported.

Officials said nothing suspicious had been found so far.

The threats come as security arrangements have been tightened across Delhi ahead of Independence Day on August 15.

item.title: ‘Batwara 1947’ review: Dull storytelling and sharp messaging
item.description: Rajkumar Santoshi’s adaptation of the play ‘Jis Lahore Nai Vekhya, O Jamya E Nai’ is out in cinemas.
item.content:encoded:
A chunk of Sunny Deol’s career is devoted to swinging hand pumps at Pakistanis, bashing in their heads or simply bellowing at them until their eardrums burst. In Rajkumar Santoshi’s Batwara 1947, Deol is in a different zone and a different register.

The Hindi-Punjabi film is adapted from a play about compassion trumping communal hatred during the horrific time of Partition. Even Sunny Deol, then, must behave.

Deol plays Sikandar, a Muslim businessman from Meerut who flees to Lahore after being targetted by Hindu rioters. Sikandar, his wife Hamida (Preity Zinta) and daughter Tanno (Khushi Hajare) enter the mansion allotted to them, only to find an elderly Hindu woman there.

The house belongs to Durgavati (Shabana Azmi). Her own son and his family are missing. Durgavati refuses to leave until her son returns.

The domestic quandary is soon eclipsed by the antics of the fanatic politician Yaqub (Abhimanyu Singh), who wants to purge the neighbourhood of its Hindu past. Adding to Sikandar’s woes is his son Javed (Karan Deol), who has been catalysed by the carnage he witnessed back in Meerut and is on Yaqub’s side.

item.title: Census 2027: Caste, Covid-19 vaccination status among 40 questions notified by Centre
item.description: This will be the first time in independent India that caste will be enumerated across communities.
item.content:encoded:
The Census 2027 will ask respondents if they belong to a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, and will also include an open-ended question for other communities about the caste that they belong to.

This will be the first time in independent India that caste will be enumerated across communities. Until now, Census exercises only recorded the population of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

Among the 40 questions notified on Friday are also those seeking information on the place where respondents received their Covid-19 vaccination, the total number of bank accounts they hold and digital literacy. The form also seeks information on Aadhaar numbers, mobile numbers, passport numbers and voter IDs.

The population enumeration phase of the census will take place from September 1 to September 30 in Ladakh and snow-bound non-synchronous areas of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, according to a gazette notification issued earlier this month. The online self-enumeration window for the second phase will be open from August 17 to August 31.

It will be conducted in other parts of the country in February 2027.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘Simple Thinking: Tackling Problems with Simplicity’, by Mukesh Sud.
item.content:encoded:
Rahul Narayan is a dreamer.

As a child, he loved watching Carl Sagan’s TV series, Cosmos. Later, it was Star Trek. Finally, Star Wars, the show that was avidly followed by an entire generation of space enthusiasts.

If you have seen an episode of Star Trek, you will remember Captain James Kirk’s mission for the Starship Enterprise:

Space, the final frontier … To explore strange new worlds, to seek out new life and new civilisations, to boldly go where no man has gone before.

The cast of Star Trek had Montgomery Scott as chief engineer. Scotty, with his quaint Scottish accent, was constantly getting everyone out of trouble. Once, after out-drinking an alien intruder, he had to repair the Enterprise while drunk.

Remember Captain Kirk’s catchphrase, “Beam me up, Scotty”, when he wanted to be teleported back to the Enterprise?

Those were the 1980s.

Rahul realised that while dreaming of space and extraterrestrial life might keep him awake at night, it could not become a career. So he studied computer science. Later, after settling into a job, Rahul’s dream of adventures in outer space never really went away.

item.title: Green India Mission fell short by nearly 98% in increasing forest cover: CAG
item.description: This was due to poor financial planning and non-alignment with existing state and central schemes, the Comptroller and Auditor General said in a report.
item.content:encoded:
The Comptroller and Auditor General has flagged that the forest cover increased by only 0.03 million hectares against a target of 1.4 million hectares in the last 10 years under the Green India Mission, reported The Times of India on Thursday. This is a shortfall of 97.5% from the target.

Launched in February 2014, the Green India Mission is an initiative under the National Action Plan on Climate Change to protect, restore, and enhance the forest cover of India.

The audit report tabled in Parliament on Wednesday said that the shortfall in implementing the mission was due to poor financial planning and non-alignment with existing state and central schemes, reported Hindustan Times.

There was also a lack of monitoring of the interventions made under the mission, according to The Times of India.

The report covered interventions made under the mission in 16 states and Union territories for which financial targets between the financial years 2015-’16 and 2024-’25 were approved by the Ministry of Environment.

It pointed out that improvement of forest cover quality was seen in only 0.1 million hectares, as compared to a target of 1.4 million hectares. This marked a shortfall of 91.8%.

item.title: Rajasthan Cabinet approves UCC bill mandating registration of live-in relationships, polygamy ban
item.description: It is the fifth Bharatiya Janata Party-ruled state to move towards implementing a common personal law framework.
item.content:encoded:
The Rajasthan Cabinet on Thursday approved a bill on Uniform Civil Code to ban polygamy and make the registration of marriages and divorces mandatory within 60 days, The Hindu reported.

The bill, approved ahead of the imposition of the model code of conduct for the upcoming panchayat and local body elections, will be introduced in the Assembly during its monsoon session beginning on August 20

Rajasthan is the fifth Bharatiya Janata Party-ruled state to move towards implementing a common personal law framework.

The Uniform Civil Code aims to introduce a common set of laws governing marriage, divorce, succession and adoption for all citizens. Currently, such personal affairs of different religions are based on community-specific laws, largely derived from religious scripture.

The Rajasthan bill has proposed provisions to establish equal property rights for sons and daughters across religions, irrespective of their personal laws, reported The Hindu.

The bill also proposes mandatory registration or written intimation of the beginning and end of live-in relationships.

The Uniform Civil Code would not apply to Scheduled Tribes and communities whose customary rights are protected under the Constitution, the newspaper quoted minister Jogaram Patel as saying.

item.title: In Pakistan, Prisoner No 804 seems to be everywhere
item.description: By jailing former Prime Minister Imran Khan, the country’s establishment aimed to doom him to irrelevance. But he has rendered him more relevant than ever.
item.content:encoded:
It wasn’t unlike a solitary vigil.

On August 1, a social media post appeared showing a woman standing outside the Karachi Press Club, holding a painted portrait of Imran Khan, bearing the words: “Imran Khan ko riha karo”, free Imran Khan, and “Hamara leader hamen wapas dedo”, give our leader back to us.

The image of her quiet defiance elided with the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf’s reignited street mobilisation, marking their leader’s three-year anniversary in prison.

Together, these instances illuminate a peculiar paradox: three years of incarceration instead of diminishing the former Pakistani prime minister’s symbolic appeal seem to actually have bolstered it.

Pakistan’s political playbook has long been recycled. Something drives a wedge between a political leader and the establishment. What follows is familiar: some combination of dismissal, disqualification, imprisonment or exile, with the eventual aim of irrelevance. Once enough time has passed and the political storm settles, an accommodation is usually reached.

The case of Khan somewhat unsettled the playbook. Khan’s own ascent to power was hardly predictable. Cricketing fame was followed by philanthropy and eventually politics, despite his initial reluctance to enter the field. item.title: Uttarakhand: Seven killed after water, debris enters tunnel being constructed in Chamoli
item.description: While 21 workers have been pulled out of the site, information about one is not yet available.
item.content:encoded:
Seven workers were killed and 14 others were injured on Thursday after water and debris entered a tunnel being constructed at a hydroelectric project site in Uttarakhand’s Chamoli district, reported The Hindu.

Twenty-two workers had been trapped inside the tunnel of the Tehri Hydro Development Corporation-owned Vishnugad-Pipalkoti Hydroelectric Project. Of these, 21 have been pulled out. Information about the remaining one worker is not yet available, reported the newspaper.

The tunnel was being constructed by the Hindustan Construction Company.

The incident was reported around 7.05 pm, The Hindu quoted the State Disaster Response Force as saying. Soon after, teams from the Indian Army, Indo-Tibetan Border Police, National Disaster Response Force and SDRF started a rescue operation at the spot. The police and the Central Industrial Security Force were also involved.

Additional teams would be deployed if needed, PTI quoted Vinod Kumar Suman, secretary of the Disaster Management and Rehabilitation Department, as saying.

Chamoli has been receiving heavy rainfall over the past several days.

On Monday, a bridge in the Niti Valley was swept away amid strong river currents due to rising water levels.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘Aryan Pasha: The Untold Story of India’s First Transgender Bodybuilding Champion’, by Apra Kuchhal.

The year 2000, the turn of the century, proved to be a landmark in many ways. The world did not end, as it was predicted. With the arrival of the internet in the 1990s, unverified news and hoaxes were doing the rounds. One claim held that the year, nicknamed Y2K, would witness a “millennium bug” that would cause chaos globally. Planes were expected to fall from the sky, computers were to reset themselves and missiles were to fire on their own. But like many doomsday prophesies, this one fell flat as well.

Naiyla’s world, however, did crumble around her in the years that followed.

Despite the anger, altercations and questions about her gender, Naiyla had not been able to accept life as a girl. She knew she was a boy, but people around her were hell-bent on proving otherwise. She kept the reality of her body buried deep inside by wearing boys’ clothes, keeping her hair short and hanging around with boys. On the eve of Indian Independence Day, the reminder issued by Justice RH Jackson in the United States feels unusually close to home. “Freedom to differ is not limited to things that do not matter much,” he said.

Universities are supposed to be institutions where that freedom is exercised vigorously – law universities especially so. Students are trained to question power and ask institutions to justify what they do. That makes the controversy that exploded at NALSAR University of Law in Hyderabad this week especially ironic.

On Thursday, a series of events that had started with an internal representation by graduating students objecting to a proposal to invite the chief justice of India to be the chief guest at their convocation prompted an action that was completely arbitrary.

The invitation to Justice Surya Kant had been opposed because of his reported response to a petition about alleged police brutality against young protesters marching to Parliament in Delhi on July 20. item.title: ‘The End of Oak Street’ review: A crisp and efficient survival thriller
item.description: David Robert Mitchell’s film stars Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor.
item.content:encoded:
It’s 1982, the year Steven Spielberg’s E.T. The Extra Terrestrial came out, three years before the first Back to the Future movie, and 11 years before the inaugural Jurassic Park film. This is the year in which a wormhole brings dinosaurs and other prehistoric creatures into the backyards of an American suburban town

The overnight arrival of the intruders adds to the drama within a boilerplate American family. Denise (Anne Hathaway) and Greg (Ewan McGregor) have a mildly strained marriage, and are keeping it together for the sake of their teenaged children Audrey (Maisy Stella) and Brian (Christian Convery). Faced with rampaging, perpetually hungry animals, the Platts muster together every available resource to escape. Only, they can’t.

David Robert Mitchell’s The End of Oak Street is an old-fashioned survival thriller that could well have been released in 1982 itself. While sketchy about the science behind the sudden appearance of creatures that are straight out of a palaeontology textbook, the film delivers on the undeniable thrill of watching people run for their lives.

The scale is never overwhelming. The visual effects are clean rather than being distracting. There are barely any extraneous characters or sub-plots.

item.title: Why disability support still evades those with blood disorders

Suryodaya Kumhar’s medical diagnosis came about through a stroke of luck. The six-year-old, who lives in Dhatkidi village in Jharkhand’s West Singhbhum district, periodically suffered from severe joint and muscle pain, and extreme fatigue. His parents had taken him to numerous doctors, but they had not been able to provide a clear diagnosis or treatment.

His eldest sister Soni, who is 16 years old, had also shown the same symptoms for years. She was often confined to her bed, and missed out on a few months of school every year. “I love to study, so I still manage to do well,” Soni said. “But will such episodes continue for the rest of my life?”

item.title: What is Gen Z’s dark and nonsensical humor trying to say?
item.description: It is less about moral values but the product of a desire to engage in more authentic conversations about what they believe.
item.content:encoded:
After Luigi Mangione was arrested in December 2024 in connection with the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, the internet did what it often does: It turned something serious into a joke.

Although Mangione has pleaded not guilty to second-degree murder in New York and to federal stalking charges, viral memes at the time romanticised him as a popular – and incredibly attractive – man of the people who made corporate elites within the American health insurance industry afraid.

Some of these memes adhered to conventional forms of political satire. One, for example, quoted a speech from the movie A Bug’s Life in which a villainous grasshopper argues for the need to punish the movie’s ant protagonist to keep the other ants in line. In this meme, the political point was clear: Elites preserve power by making examples of insignificant ants who dare to challenge them.

The point was less clear with other memes, including celebrations of Mangione’s fashion-forward shackled ankles in court and mock Burger King advertisements referencing the fact that a McDonald’s employee had been the one to call law enforcement on him: “Burger King: We won’t turn you in to the Feds.” Rather than being ironic, they are unserious.

item.title: Sugarcane powers India’s rural economy but climate change is affecting yield
item.description: The crop sustains millions of farmers but concerns are growing over its water demands as the changing weather poses challenges.
item.content:encoded:
Sugarcane cultivation across parts of India’s Deccan Plateau is becoming more productive. But, it is also becoming more vulnerable to climate variability, a new long-term study finds.

Sugarcane has long shaped India’s rural economy. It powers sugar mills, supports ethanol and bioenergy production, and sustains millions of farmers. But the crop is also at the centre of mounting concerns over water use, particularly in semi-arid regions facing recurrent droughts and groundwater stress.

The study analysed 22 years of sugarcane production trends across five districts in Maharashtra and Karnataka to understand how cultivation, yields and production patterns have changed under varying climatic conditions.

“We noticed that sugarcane cultivation in Maharashtra and Karnataka was increasingly being affected by climatic variability, even though it remains one of the most important economic activities across the Deccan Plateau,” says Krishna Kumar from the Department of Applied Science and Humanities at MIT-ADT University, Pune, and one of the study’s researchers.

Across climate zones

Sugarcane production trends in India have been studied extensively at national and state levels, but long-term district-level analyses incorporating weather variability remain limited.

item.title: Nisha da Cunha (1934-2026): An inspirational teacher and writer of things usually left unsaid
item.description: Her literary contribution is particularly significant for its topicality today, writes a former student.
item.content:encoded:
Some people come to us to definitively shape who we later become. Call it providence, fate, destiny, chance or sheer good luck, but Professor Nisha da Cunha, who died on August 11, was one such provocateur in my life.

My recollections of her are perhaps common to every student of English Literature at St Xavier's College of the mid- and late 1970s – the commanding air, the measured diction while reading a text aloud in the classroom, trademark poise, impatience with students who "showed off" and her passionate guidance of those she believed had potential.

item.title: What decolonising economics can look like
item.description: The discipline has largely overlooked how colonialism, empire and unequal power have shaped economic development.
item.content:encoded:
Economics shapes many aspects of our daily lives, from the prices we pay to the policies governments adopt. Yet many of the ideas taught as universal principles of economics emerged from a narrow historical context and have rarely been examined through a decolonial lens.

A recently published book, Decolonizing Economics, argues that economics is long overdue for decolonisation. Its authors contend that the discipline has largely overlooked how colonialism, empire and unequal power shaped the development of modern economies and the economic theories used to explain them.

Decolonising economics means rethinking how we understand economic development and inequality. Rather than explaining prosperity through technology, markets and scientific progress, it examines how colonisation, resource extraction and exploited labour shaped today’s wealthy economies while contributing to underdevelopment elsewhere.

At its core, it’s about shifting away from an economy that benefits the elite to one that builds people’s capabilities.

As an economics professor, I’ve been restructuring my teaching based on my scholarship on critical microeconomics, critical macroeconomics and alternative ways to build the economy.

At a time when India was being courted by the Cold War superpowers, Kerala was one state that overwhelmingly leaned towards Moscow rather than Washington DC.

The Hindustan Times said its sound metrers clocked more than 100 decibels as trucks carrying large sound systems moved through residential areas near Kalindi Kunj and Kalkaji. Between passing convoys, readings were between 80 decibels and 88 decibels.

Police officers directed traffic and assisted pilgrims, some drivers were asked to lower the volume, but no FIRs had been registered when the measurements were reported. In fact, in Uttar Pradesh, the Kanwar Yatra pilgrims were welcomes included flower petals showered from helicopters.

Why is noise during religious events sometimes a public health violation, but other times a celebration that the administration must accommodate?

India’s noise rules make no religious distinction. They require written permission for loudspeakers, set residential limits of 55 decibels by day and 45 at night, and prohibit outdoor amplification between 10 pm and 6 am. Limited festival exemptions do not remove the applicable volume limits.

Noise is a public health concern. Roadkill data for small carnivores is heavily underreported, and these records were “a matter of chance”, according to Vishnupriya Kolipakam, a Wildlife Institute of India scientist and one of the paper’s authors.

When one considers the contradictions between the Enlightenment’s stated ideals and their practical implementation, for example, if we take the case of the American Revolution, which was one of the earliest implementations of the movement inspired by Enlightenment principles such as liberty, equality, and natural rights, and note that it coexisted with chattel slavery, we find that the Enlightenment ideals functioned as an ideological framework that could also coexist with, without any disturbance in its coexistence with a profoundly unequal and racialised society. Northup, born a free Black man, who was enslaved and then later freed through legal intervention, appealed to reason and human dignity, and challenged, early on, the point being made here – that in the superficial universality of Enlightenment ideals within a racial order, Black or, by extension, coloured lives were expendable....

Noting that the complaint against Singh was filed a long time after the alleged sexual harassment, Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate Ashwini Panwar of Rouse Avenue Courts also said that the wrestlers’ accusations against Singh appeared to be rehearsed, well-practised and planted.

In January 2023, several Indian wrestlers, including medallists Sakshi Malik, Bajrang Punia and Vinesh Phogat, launched a protest against Singh, accusing him of intimidation and sexual harassment.

Seven complainants, including a minor, accused the Bharatiya Janata Party leader of demanding sexual favours for professional help on at least two occasions, and also reported 15 incidents of alleged molestation and other forms of sexual harassment.

The former MP was later cleared with respect to allegations made by one of the women.

On August 3, he and his co-accused, Vinod Tomar, were acquitted of all charges by Panwar.

He noted in his order that two of the complainants had “categorically admitted” that they were not sexually harassed by Singh, reported Bar and Bench.

item.title: Centre introduces bill in Lok Sabha to restrict states from imposing taxes on mineral rights
item.description: The bill, introduced by Union minister G Kishan Reddy on Monday, also seeks to empower the Union government to regulate mineral-bearing lands.
item.content:encoded:
The Union government on Monday introduced a bill in the Lok Sabha to restrict states from imposing additional tax on mineral rights, PTI reported.

The bill also seeks to empower the Union government to regulate mineral-bearing lands in accordance with the parameters prescribed under the 1957 Mines and Minerals Development and Regulation Act, the news agency reported.

Union Minister of Coal and Mines G Kishan Reddy introduced the 2026 Mines and Minerals Development and Regulation Amendment Bill amid protests by Opposition members.

According to the bill, “no tax, cess or such other levy (by whatever name called) shall be imposed by the state government on mineral rights”.

The proposed provisions would cover mineral-bearing lands, with their applicability determined by factors such as the quantity or value of minerals, royalty payments or other prescribed criteria. Such lands would be subject to conditions and restrictions specified by the Union government, PTI reported.

The bill, however, clarifies that any tax, cess or other levy on mineral rights or mineral-bearing lands that was paid to or collected by a state government before the provisions take effect “shall not be liable to be refunded”.

Reddy said that the amendments seek to “provide certainty, stability and predictability in the fiscal regime in the mineral sector,” the news agency reported.

item.title: Allahabad HC orders Rs 25 lakh compensation to sisters confined by father for converting to Islam
item.description: Depriving them of their liberty was ‘an exceptionally grave and egregious violation of constitutional rights’, held the court.
item.content:encoded:
The Allahabad High Court has ordered the Uttar Pradesh government and the father of two women, who voluntarily converted to Islam, to pay them Rs 25 lakh in compensation for unlawfully confining them.

In a judgement delivered on August 6, Justice Sandeep Jain also ordered that the sisters be released. ,

Jain held that they were liable to get compensation for the “unlawful deprivation” of their fundamental rights. Their confinement amounted to “an exceptionally grave and egregious violation of constitutional rights”, he added.

The two sisters, aged 20 and 35, had told the court that they had voluntarily converted from Hinduism to Islam and decided to marry as per their own wishes, which was their fundamental right. They denied having changed their faith because of force, fraud or “undue influence”.

The sisters alleged that their father had confined them inside their paternal home after they converted.

In his judgement, Jain said that he interacted independently with both women and found that their responses were “spontaneous, coherent and unequivocal”. The judge held that the sisters, as adults, had the legal capacity to take decisions about their lives.

item.title: 132 killed as 7.4-magnitude earthquake hits Colombia
item.description: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, who was sworn in only three days ago, has declared a state of emergency.
item.content:encoded:
At least 132 persons were killed after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia on Monday, stated the Colombian Association of Capital Cities, a non-profit organisation. Additionally, 483 persons were injured.

The toll is likely to rise as several persons are feared trapped under collapsed buildings, reported the BBC.

The earthquake struck at 7.34 am local time and damaged at least 1,500 buildings, reported AFP. The epicentre was near the village of San José del Palmar, in Chocó province.

The cities of Cali, Pereira, Quibdo and Manizales were most affected by the quake. It was also felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama.

This was the strongest earthquake recorded in Colombia in the 21st century and it was followed by several aftershocks, AP quoted the country’s Geological Service as saying.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, who was sworn in only three days ago, has declared a state of emergency.

“We aren’t going to leave people alone,” he was quoted as saying by the AP. “They are in our hearts and we are going to tend to people with our full determination.”

Hospitals in five Colombian cities were put on red alert Monday. A nighttime curfew has been declared in Cali.

Six airports have suspended operations, according to AFP.

item.title: The ‘left-behind’ India: Global trade deals can have disruptive political consequences
item.description: The economic benefits are concentrated in a few places, deepening regional inequality and prompting migration which fuels nativist backlash.
item.content:encoded:
Amid talk of fractures in world trade, India continues to pursue globalisation as an economic development strategy. After a decade without any trade deals, India signed agreements with the European Union, United Kingdom, and New Zealand over 2025 and 2026, and is continuing negotiations with the US and other regions, signaling a renewed commitment to global economic integration. Most analyses of these agreements emphasise their geopolitical implications, especially for India’s emerging-power status and strategic relationship with the US, China, and Russia.

But these new deals will also contribute to the transformation of India’s domestic political economy. From India’s initial liberalisation in 1991, to its (re)emergence as a major exporter of textiles and apparel, to its dominant position in information technology services, globalisation has reshaped economic opportunity, social conflict, and political outcomes.

This transformation has touched areas intensely integrated with the global economy, but also localities that are little exposed to world markets. These new agreements, which grant extensive access to lucrative export markets, will likely catalyse deeper connections between India and the global economy.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘From the Depth of the Mould: Meera Mukherjee (1923-1998), A Centenary Tribute’, edited by Tapati Guha-Thakurta.
item.content:encoded:
A gigantic female figure opens a window high above her head to look out into the sky. Her face is turned away from viewers as her massive arms pull up the shutters. When this work by Meera Mukherjee was first exhibited in the galleries of the Birla Academy of Art and Culture, Kolkata, in 1993, it carried the title Akash [Sky]. The centre-piece of that exhibition, it towered towards the ceiling of the room, appearing to push itself out into the open. Like her other larger-than-life figures, this sculpture also seemed to demand its place under the open skies, although its permanent home would become the gallery of another Birla art museum in Hyderabad. Like its counterparts of similar or bigger scale, the figure too is made in many parts that were cast in a furnace in molten metal out of clay core units and elaborately striated wax moulds, with its limbs, torso and head later welded together. However, the judge criticised senior US Justice Department official Trent McCotter’s conduct as “highly unusual” in the case.

“The fact that McCotter came to this decision [to drop the charges] largely in collaboration with defense counsel, and seemingly without input from the FBI [Federal Bureau of Investigation] and SEC [Securities Exchange Commission] agents who investigated the alleged misconduct, or [prosecutors] who brought the case, appears to be highly unusual,” he wrote.

item.title: ‘She had stepped out to buy food’: Another Bengali woman forcibly pushed to Bangladesh from Mumbai
item.description: The police acted against Sahida Fakir despite her family submitting her birth and school certificates, her voter ID card and a land title, her husband said.

On the evening of July 19, Sahida Fakir headed to a market near her home in Navi Mumbai to buy food for dinner, leaving her 10-year-old son at home. She has not returned home since.

A few hours later, her husband Jumman Fakir got a call from the Mumbai police’s Chembur crime branch. Sahida had been detained on “suspicion of being an illegal immigrant”.

Fakir rushed to the police station.

Sahida told him that the police personnel had forcibly dragged her to a building where persons suspected to be “illegal immigrants” were reportedly being detained. “They took away the food she bought, her phone and Aadhaar card,” Fakir said. “She was detained because she was a Bengali.”

item.title: Nairobi is bulldozing the Kibera settlement for a housing project, but who really benefits?
item.description: Kenya’s plan for affordable homes aims to redevelop one of the country’s most visible symbols of urban poverty.
item.content:encoded:
Bulldozers and construction crews are reshaping parts of Nairobi’s best-known informal settlement, Kibera. In a video shared by President William Ruto, new apartment blocks rise alongside existing corrugated-iron structures, while new roads cut through the settlement. The message is clear: Kenya’s affordable housing programme is bringing modern housing to one of the country’s most visible symbols of urban poverty.

The redevelopment forms part of Ruto’s broader affordable housing programme, which aims to deliver 200,000 housing units annually, combining social housing, affordable homes and market-rate units. By March 2026, government figures indicated that 8,367 units had been completed since Ruto took office in September 2022, with many more at various stages of construction across the country. Completed units therefore remain well below the programme’s stated annual target.

Supporters see it as a long-overdue investment in urban infrastructure and housing. Critics, however, have challenged the compulsory levy used to finance the programme: employees pay 1.5% of their gross monthly salary, matched by a 1.5% employer contribution, while people outside formal employment pay 1.5% of their gross income. They have also raised concerns about whether the homes will be affordable to lower-income households and allocated transparently.

item.title: Rural jobs fall nearly 50% in first month of VB-G RAM G: Report
item.description: The employment generation figures in July were the lowest in the last five years for both households and person-days.
item.content:encoded:
Employment generated under the government’s new rural job guarantee scheme fell by nearly half in July, the first month since it replaced the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme, The Indian Express reported on Monday.

Only 7.6 crore person-days were generated under the Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission Gramin Act, or VB-G RAM G, in July, as compared to 15.3 crore in the same month last year under MGNREGA, the newspaper cited official data.

A person-day refers to the amount of work done by one person in one working day. This means that a 20 person-day project can be completed by 20 people in one day, or one person in 20 days

The number of households that availed the rural employment guarantee scheme also fell by 51.4% to 68.9 lakh in July, compared with 1.4 crore under the old scheme in the same month last year.

The July figures for both households and person-days were the lowest in the last five years, reported The Indian Express.

The new scheme came into effect on July 1, replacing the two-decade-old MGNREGA.
